newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to slash troop strength in Africa - paper.
newsitem.headline: France to slash troop strength in Africa - paper.

text.p: France's leftist government has endorsed and broadened a plan by the previous centre-right administration to cut military strength in Africa, the newspaper Le Monde reported on Saturday.
Officials at the prime minister's office and the defence ministry refused to comment on the report, which was the latest sign of France's desire to loosen its ties with former African colonies.

Le Monde said the six-week-old government of Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin planned to cut the number of French troops on the continent gradually from 8,350 to 5,000 and to close one of the six bases which they use.

The base to close would be that in Bangui, N'Djamena or Freetown, it said. Jospin and Gaullist President Jacques Chirac might take a decision on the base before a visit to Africa by Defence Minister Alain Richard due in late July.

The plan first unveiled by Richard's predecessor, Charles Millon, followed planned reforms to create all-professional armed forces by 2002 that would be easier to send outside France's borders. Professionals already make up most of the air force and navy and a sizeable part of the army.
Le Monde said each of the five bases to remain in operation in Africa would have a thousand-strong force made up of members of the three armed forces and the paramilitary gendarmerie.
Troops would be sent to the bases on four-month shifts rather than longer periods as was previously the case, it said, ensuring savings for the defence budget.

France has intervened dozens of times across Africa since granting independence to its former colonies in the early 1960s, mostly to prop up governments friendly to Paris but also in Zaire and Rwanda which were Belgian possessions.
The Socialist Party was long critical of France's African policy which it said perpetuated neo-colonial relations and backed dictators.

Recurrent reports in Paris newspapers say French leaders, including the Socialists, believe the United States wishes to replace France as the virtual "protecting power" in the region whose raw materials represent wide economic potential.

Cooperation Minister Charles Josselin told a news conference this month: "Today's Africa is not what it was in the 1960s, the French army is itself being reorganised and the notion of mobility has changed."
